title: SPECIMEN 001
name: Bottarga

description.short: Salt-cured grey mullet roe, traditionally produced in Sardinia.
description.long: Prepared for centuries along Mediterranean coasts, bottarga is made from the roe of the grey mullet (Mugil cephalus). Carefully salted, pressed and naturally dried, it has become one of Sardinia's most distinctive culinary traditions, particularly around the Cabras Lagoon.

museumNotes.title: Museum Notes
museumNotes.text: Although today it is considered a delicacy, bottarga originated as a practical method of preserving fish roe. The traditional production process has remained remarkably consistent over generations, relying on salt, pressure, fresh air and time rather than modern industrial techniques.

fieldObservation.title: Field Observation
fieldObservation.text: The Cabras Lagoon, on the western coast of Sardinia, provides one of the most renowned environments for grey mullet fishing. Local knowledge, seasonal rhythms and artisanal methods continue to shape the production of bottarga today.

facts: Prepared from the roe of grey mullet (Mugil cephalus).
Naturally cured using sea salt, pressure and air.
One of the most iconic traditional foods of Sardinia.

title: SPECIMEN 002
name: Welwitschia

hero.title: Welwitschia mirabilis
hero.subtitle: The ancient plant that never stops growing.

description.short: An ancient desert plant that survives where almost nothing else can.
description.long: Welwitschia mirabilis is one of the world's strangest plants. Growing exclusively in the Namib Desert, it has adapted to survive where rainfall is scarce, temperatures are extreme and life is exceptionally difficult. Each individual produces only two leaves throughout its entire existence. They never stop growing, becoming long ribbons sculpted by centuries of wind and sand.

museumNotes.title: Museum Notes
museumNotes.text: First described in 1859 by Austrian botanist Friedrich Welwitsch, the species puzzled scientists from the very beginning. Although it resembles a giant bundle of leaves, the plant belongs to one of the oldest surviving lineages of seed plants. Instead of depending on rainfall alone, it survives thanks to deep roots, slow growth and moisture carried inland by Atlantic fog.

fieldObservation.title: Living in the Namib
fieldObservation.text: The Namib Desert is one of the oldest deserts on Earth. Despite extreme temperatures and almost complete absence of rain, Welwitschia survives through a combination of deep roots, slow growth and moisture gathered from coastal fog.

facts: Some Welwitschia plants alive today began growing before Christopher Columbus reached the Americas.
Throughout its entire life, the plant produces only two leaves.
Rather than relying on rainfall alone, Welwitschia absorbs moisture from Atlantic fog.
